chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Whoever precedes in supplication — it will be answered for him when affliction befalls him, and the angels will say, 'A well-known voice, not veiled from the sky';
and whoever does not precede in supplication — it will not be answered for him when affliction befalls him, and the angels will say, 'This is a voice we do not recognize.'

key_terms.الْبَلَاءُ: Affliction, tribulation, divine trial — used in classical Arabic for any serious hardship that tests a person
key_terms.تَقَدَّمَ فِي الدُّعَاءِ: To precede/advance in supplication — making du'a consistently before any calamity, in times of ease and wellbeing
key_terms.صَوْتٌ مَعْرُوفٌ: A recognized/familiar voice — the angel's testimony that this person's supplications are known and established in the heavens
key_terms.يُحْجَبْ عَنِ السَّمَاءِ: Veiled/blocked from the sky — the supplication does not reach the divine realm; it is blocked or turned back

ai.seo_question: Why should Muslims make du'a before calamity strikes in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches that making du'a in times of ease and wellbeing — before any affliction arrives — establishes one's voice as known and recognized by the angels. When hardship then strikes, that supplication is answered readily. By contrast, one who only turns to God in desperation, having neglected du'a in times of ease, finds their plea unrecognized by the angels and unanswered. This hadith reflects the Shia emphasis on habitual, consistent worship as the foundation of a relationship with God that bears fruit in times of need.
